Set trade policy, such as tariffs and trade blocs
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional country of Zandia. Governments want economic growth, jobs, stable prices and safe consumers. Ask: how can a new road help a business? Lower transport costs, better access to customers. Ask: how can higher tax hurt? Lower profit or higher prices. Teacher: do not discuss real governments' policies as facts; keep fictional.

teach.heading: Tariffs and taxes
teach.note: Model a tariff calculation. Ask who pays: the importer, who may pass it on to customers. Limits: a government cannot spend more than it raises without borrowing; high tax may reduce enterprise. Point out how a business pays taxes honestly and on time as a matter of trust.

model.problem: Zandia imposes a 10% tariff on imported bicycles. Samir imports 200 bicycles at 120 pounds each. Calculate the tariff and the new cost per bicycle.
model.answer: Tariff 2,400 pounds; cost per bicycle 132 pounds

teach.heading: Interest rates
teach.note: Compare effects of a rise in rates. Businesses with loans pay more; customers who borrow spend less; savers may save more. So demand falls for expensive goods bought on credit. A fall helps borrowers. Then the Islamic note: riba (رِبَا, interest) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba); Islamic finance uses partnership (musharakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murabahah, مُرَابَحَة) instead. Interest rates are taught as knowledge of how the wider economy works.

teach.heading: STEP factors
bullets: Social: tastes, population, attitudes
Technological: new machines, online sales
Environmental: climate, waste, sustainability
Political: government changes and laws
teach.note: Give examples for Zandia: an ageing population increases demand for care homes (social); AI tools change office work (technological); a plastic ban affects packaging (environmental); a new government changes tax rules (political). Ask pupils to name one threat and one opportunity for a bakery from each factor. These influence decisions such as location, product and price.

teach.heading: Check: tariff
teach.note: Answer D. A tariff raises the cost of imported goods. A and B are not tariff effects.

check.q: What is the most direct effect of a tariff on an importer?
check.why: A tariff is a tax on imports so the importer's costs rise.

teach.heading: Evaluating external change
bullets: List the factor and who it affects
Assess how big the effect is
Consider short and long term
Recommend action: adapt, absorb, or change plans
teach.note: Practise on a scenario: a rise in interest rates from 4% to 7% on a 50,000 pounds loan: interest cost rises from 2,000 to 3,500. Discuss action: cut costs, raise prices, overpay loan. Reach a decision. A business that adapts survives; one that ignores change may fail.

practice: Loan of 80,000 pounds. Interest rate rises from 5% to 8%. Calculate the extra annual interest.
Name one STEP factor and its effect on a clothes shop.
Explain how a new road could help a business.
independent: Core: Sort ten events into social, technological, environmental or political.
Extend: Explain two effects of a tax rise on a restaurant.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Zandia raises interest rates and introduces a plastic packaging ban. Which is more serious for a small food manufacturer, and why?
exit: Define tariff.
State one effect of an interest rate rise on consumers.
Big question: how can decisions made by governments or society change a business overnight? Give one example.
lessons.homework: Find one news story that affects businesses and classify it as a STEP factor.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a STEP sorting grid. EAL: pre-teach tariff, legislation. Stretch: weigh short-term against long-term effects.

lessons.title: Business success and failure
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you know when a business has really succeeded?
objectives: Describe measures of success: revenue, market share, customer satisfaction, profit, growth, owner and employee satisfaction
Explain reasons for failure: cash flow, lack of finance, being uncompetitive, failure to adapt
Make a reasoned judgement on a business's success
successCriteria: All: name four success measures and two causes of failure
Most: calculate revenue growth and profit margin to measure success
Some: evaluate a business using several measures and reach a conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: English: structured argument and evaluation; Maths: percentage change
lessons.smsc: Moral: success judged by honest earning, fairness and service, not only by profit

keywords.def: achieving a business's aims and objectives
when a business cannot continue or achieves poor results
how well customers' needs and expectations are met
an increase in the size of the business, such as sales or number of outlets
to change in response to new conditions

starter: State one effect of a rise in interest rates on a business.

teach.heading: Measures of success
bullets: Revenue and profit
Market share and growth
Customer satisfaction
Owner and employee satisfaction
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Kite Cafe. Ask pupils: if Kite Cafe makes 20,000 profit but staff are unhappy and customers complain, is it successful? Draw out that success can be judged by different measures and different stakeholders. Link to Islamic ethos: honest and fair dealing matter beyond profit; the teacher may expand.

teach.heading: Worked example: measuring success
teach.note: Model with two years of data. Ask: which stakeholder cares about each measure? Evaluate: revenue growth is good but the profit margin fell, suggesting costs rose faster. Pupils should comment on both.

model.problem: Kite Cafe: Year 1 revenue 200,000, profit 30,000. Year 2 revenue 240,000, profit 33,600. Calculate revenue growth and profit margin each year.
steps: Compare: revenue up but margin down
model.answer: Revenue grew 20%; margin fell from 15% to 14%

teach.heading: Why businesses fail
bullets: Cash flow problems or lack of finance
Uncompetitive: prices or quality worse than rivals
Failure to adapt to changing tastes or technology
Poor management or unexpected shocks
teach.note: Link to earlier units: cash flow forecasts, market research, location. Give Kite Cafe's story: a rival opens opposite with cheaper coffee, but Kite does not respond and delays paying suppliers: cash shortage. Ask how it could have avoided failure. Honest early warnings to lenders and suppliers is better than hiding problems.

teach.heading: Success or failure: the evidence
teach.note: Table to use as an evaluation template. Pupils use evidence from each measure. Note some measures may conflict: profit up but customer satisfaction down. A final judgement must say which measure matters most for that business and why.

teach.heading: Check: reason for failure
teach.note: Answer B. Not responding to changes is failure to adapt. A and C are strengths.

check.q: A video shop keeps renting DVDs while customers move to streaming, and closes. This is mainly:
check.why: Ignoring changes in customers' behaviour and technology is failure to adapt.

teach.heading: Writing an evaluation
bullets: State the measure and evidence
Link to the business and its aims
Weigh the measures against each other
Give a clear final judgement
teach.note: Model the structure for 20-mark questions: point, evidence, explanation, counter-point, judgement. Tell pupils that the examiner wants a decision supported by evidence, not a list. Use Kite Cafe: a conclusion could be 'Moderately successful, because revenue and profit are growing, but customer and staff satisfaction need attention for long-term survival.'

practice: Revenue rose from 150,000 to 183,000 pounds. Calculate the percentage growth.
State two reasons why a business might fail.
Explain why profit alone may not show success.
independent: Core: Use a data table for a fictional business to complete five success measures and judge each.
Extend: Explain why customer satisfaction matters for long-term success.
Stretch: Evaluate (20-mark style plan): 'Profit is the best measure of a business's success.' Plan an answer with two points for, two against and a conclusion.
exit: Name three measures of success.
State one reason for business failure.
Big question: how do you know a business has really succeeded? Answer with one measure and one reason it might mislead.
lessons.homework: Choose a local business and write a short paragraph judging its success, using two measures.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a writing frame for evaluation. EAL: vocabulary support for success measures. Stretch: write a full 20-mark answer.

lessons.title: Why motivation matters to a business
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a business gain when its workers want to do a good job?
objectives: Define motivation and explain how it helps a business attract and retain employees
Explain how motivation improves productivity
Calculate labour turnover and productivity to judge the effect of motivation
successCriteria: All: define motivation and state two benefits to a business
Most: calculate productivity and labour turnover
Some: evaluate whether a motivation scheme is worth its cost
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and ratios; PSHE: wellbeing at work
lessons.smsc: Social and moral: sincerity of intention (ikhlas) and fair, respectful treatment of staff

keywords.def: the desire or willingness of employees to work hard and do a good job
output per worker in a given time
keeping employees so that they stay with the business
the percentage of employees who leave in a year
employees missing work without good reason

starter: State one reason for equal opportunities law.
What is the difference between recruitment and selection?

teach.heading: What is motivation?
bullets: The reason an employee chooses to work hard
Motivated staff care about quality and customers
Low motivation means mistakes, lateness and absence
Motivation comes from pay and from how people are treated
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Noor Printing, twelve staff who print and deliver orders. Ask: when did you last work hard on something? What made you want to? Elicit pay, recognition, interest, being trusted, being treated fairly. Link to intentions: the same work done with sincerity and care tends to be better work. The theories of Herzberg, Maslow and Taylor and the pay and non-pay methods come in another lesson; today is about why it matters.

teach.heading: Benefits to the business
teach.note: Use the cycle. Walk round it: motivated staff stay longer, so the business spends less on recruiting and training; experienced staff produce more and better work; better quality pleases customers; more sales support pay and a good workplace. Attract: a business with a good reputation as an employer receives more and better applicants. Retain: fewer leavers.
cycle: They work harder and stay longer
Customers are happier and sales grow
The business can afford better rewards

teach.heading: Worked example: measuring the effect
teach.note: Model both formulas. Productivity = output / number of employees. Labour turnover (%) = leavers in the year / average number of employees x 100 (a common formula, not listed in the spec: say so, and use as extension). Discuss what 15 per cent means: about one in seven leave each year. Then discuss cost: each leaver costs advertising, interview time and training. Do not quote real averages.

model.problem: Noor Printing has 40 employees on average. Six leave this year. Before a new reward scheme, 12 printers produce 3,000 orders a month. After, the same 12 produce 3,300. Calculate labour turnover, and productivity before and after.
model.answer: Labour turnover is 15 per cent; productivity rose from 250 to 275 orders per printer, a 10 per cent increase.

teach.heading: Check: attract and retain
teach.note: Answer B. Retaining means keeping employees. A is about recruiting new staff; C is a cost saving that has nothing to do with staying; D is about productivity not retention. Ask pupils to reword the true statement in their own words.

check.q: Which situation best shows motivation helping a business RETAIN employees?
options: More people apply for a job after an advert
Fewer experienced workers resign this year than last year
The business moves to a cheaper building
A worker completes more orders in an hour
check.why: Retaining means keeping workers, shown by fewer resignations. More applicants is attraction and more orders per hour is productivity.

teach.heading: Is it always worth it?
bullets: Rewards cost money, time and effort
A scheme must raise output or cut leavers to pay off
Not everyone is motivated by the same things
Fair treatment costs little but matters a lot
teach.note: Evaluation slide. Calculate for the class: if a scheme costs 6,000 pounds a year and replacing one leaver costs about 2,500 pounds (invented figure), the scheme pays for itself if it prevents three leavers. Ask: what else would you want to know? (Whether the leavers left for pay or for other reasons, how productivity changes.) Remind them that motivation also needs trust and respect, not just money.

practice: Calculate productivity: 4,500 meals made by 15 chefs in a week.
A cafe has 25 staff on average and 5 leave in a year. Calculate labour turnover.
Explain one reason a motivated workforce might lower costs for a business.
independent: Core: Copy and complete the cycle for a halal restaurant: show how motivated staff can lead to higher profit.
Extend: Explain two ways motivation helps a business attract and retain employees (4 marks).

Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a bakery spends 8,000 pounds a year on bonuses and free meals. Productivity rises 6 per cent and two fewer staff leave. Is the spending justified? State what else you need to know.
exit: Define motivation.
Write the productivity formula.
Big question: one reason a business gains from motivated workers.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about a job they enjoyed. Write what motivated them and how it affected their work.
lessons.send: SEND: give the formulae on cards and a step-by-step calculation frame. EAL: use pictures for retain, attract. Stretch: explore why money alone may not retain staff.

lessons.title: Human resources: planning, training, safety and industrial relations
lessons.bigQuestion: What does a business need to do to look after the people who make it work?
objectives: Describe the main tasks of the human resources department
Explain workforce planning, training, health and safety, welfare, employment issues and industrial relations
Calculate staffing needs for workforce planning
successCriteria: All: list six HR tasks
Most: explain two HR tasks using an example
Some: calculate staffing needs and judge the effect of poor industrial relations
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: calculating staff numbers; PSHE: safety and wellbeing
lessons.smsc: Moral: duty of care and fair dealing towards employees

keywords.def: working out how many staff, with which skills, the business needs
protecting people from injury and illness at work
looking after employees' wellbeing
the relationship between employers and employees or their representatives
an organisation that represents workers and negotiates with employers
matters such as contracts, pay, hours and working conditions

starter: What is productivity and how is it calculated?
Give two ways a business can motivate staff.
State one benefit of using part-time staff.

teach.heading: The HR department
teach.note: Bismillah. In a small business the owner does these jobs; in larger businesses there is a human resources (HR) department, one of the main functional areas. Context: fictional Safa Logistics, a delivery firm with 60 staff. Ask pupils to guess what HR does, then reveal the table. Recruitment and selection and training are covered in other lessons, so today link, not repeat.

head: HR task
What it involves
Example at Safa Logistics
rows: Decide how many staff and which skills are needed
Plan extra drivers before a busy period
Rest breaks, quiet room, counselling support
Meet the union about new shift times

teach.heading: Worked example: workforce planning
teach.note: Model the calculation: required hours divided by hours per worker. Then ask: what if two staff are off sick or a seasonal peak? Workforce planning is not just a number: it covers skills too (do they have licences to drive? first aid?). Discuss the cost of hiring too few (late deliveries, stressed staff) and too many (wasted wages).

model.problem: Safa Logistics expects 780 hours of delivery work a week in the busy period. Each full-time driver works 30 hours a week on the road. It has 22 drivers. How many more drivers does it need?
steps: Drivers needed = total hours / hours per driver
model.answer: Safa Logistics needs 4 more drivers (for example seasonal or temporary staff).

teach.heading: Health, safety and welfare
bullets: Employers have a legal duty to protect workers
Risk checks, safety training and protective equipment
Welfare goes beyond safety: breaks, support, facilities
Safe, cared-for staff work better and leave less often
teach.note: Do not quote specific legislation unless you can verify it; in the UK the main law is the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 (verify). The idea to teach: employers must provide a safe workplace. Welfare examples: rest areas, drinking water, flexibility for prayer times where practical, counselling help lines, sick pay. Link to the Islamic ethic of caring for those in your charge, as a value, not a ruling.

teach.heading: Industrial relations and employment issues
bullets: Good relations mean talking and listening to staff
Trade unions negotiate pay and conditions for members
Poor relations can lead to strikes and lost output
Contracts and fair conditions prevent disputes
teach.note: Define a trade union and collective bargaining (a union negotiates with the employer for a group of workers). Use the two outcomes: good industrial relations (regular meetings, listening, fair pay deals) versus poor (rumours, working to rule, strike). Discuss costs of a strike: lost production, late deliveries, damaged reputation, lost wages. Employment issues: written contract, hours, holidays, overtime, pay, promotion routes.

teach.heading: Check: which HR task?
teach.note: Answer C. Meeting union representatives to discuss shift patterns is industrial relations. A is health and safety, B is workforce planning, D is training. Ask pupils which keyword in the stem gave it away.

check.q: Safa Logistics' managers meet union representatives to agree new shift times. Which HR task is this?
check.why: Discussions with workers' representatives about conditions are industrial relations. The others deal with safety, numbers of staff or skills.

teach.heading: Linking HR to the rest of the business
teach.note: Use this as the plenary slide to link to other departments: finance (wages and budgets), marketing (staff who deal with customers need training), production (safe machines and skilled workers). Ask how a decision by HR to cut training could affect production and finance later. Revisit the big question and list the tasks pupils think matter most.
bullets: HR works with every other department
Training affects quality and safety
Workforce plans affect the wage budget
Poor welfare affects productivity and turnover

teach.heading: Dismissal, unfair dismissal, redundancy

Dismissal can be fair: for example serious misconduct, repeated lateness after warnings, or persistent poor performance after support. Unfair dismissal: no valid reason, no proper procedure, or a reason such as discrimination or joining a union. Redundancy: the JOB disappears, perhaps because demand fell or a machine replaced it. teach.heading: Cash-flow forecasts and budgets
teach.note: Show the table, which is a one-month forecast. Closing balance = opening balance + receipts - payments. The closing balance of one month becomes the opening of the next. teach.heading: Check: budget variance
teach.note: Answer A. 6,800 - 6,000 = 800 above budget, so costs are higher than planned. B reverses it, C is the budget, D is the actual figure. Pupils should say 'actual minus budget' and state whether it is above or below.

bullets: Accounts record sales, costs and assets
Used for tax, loans and decisions by owners
Marketing, HR and production all depend on finance budgets
Honest records protect trust with banks and customers
teach.note: Accounting means recording transactions and preparing financial statements (covered in the financial documents unit). teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Yasmin's Granola, a halal-certified cereal maker, selling to supermarkets and online. Marketing ties together much of what pupils learned in unit 4: research, product, price, promotion, place, packaging. Ask pupils to give one real example for each task from Yasmin's. teach.note: Production is the department that makes the goods (or provides the service). Designing new products relies on market research from marketing and on cost limits from finance. teach.note: Model the simple formula reorder level = (daily usage x lead time) + buffer stock. Lead time is the time between ordering and delivery. The buffer stock is a safety margin. keywords.def: a financial statement showing revenue, costs and profit over a period

teach.heading: Reading the income statement
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Rayyan's Halal Butchers. Construction of the statement is not required in the exam, but pupils must read and use it. Walk down the table: sales revenue, less cost of sales equals gross profit, less expenses equals operating profit. Note that the specification calls it the statement of comprehensive income; many businesses say income statement or profit and loss account. Pupils need the two profit lines.

teach.heading: Worked example: why profit fell
teach.note: Model the calculations in order. Percentage change = change / original x 100. Sales up 20 per cent but cost of sales up 30 per cent: the cost of meat and supplies grew faster than sales. Gross profit grew only 5 per cent. Expenses grew 12.5 per cent. Operating profit fell 10 per cent. Discuss decisions: negotiate with suppliers, adjust prices, reduce waste, control expenses. Emphasise using numbers in an answer.

model.problem: Using the table, find the percentage change in sales and in operating profit between Year 1 and Year 2, and say what it shows.
steps: Sales change = (180,000 - 150,000) / 150,000 x 100 = 20 per cent increase
Operating profit change = (18,000 - 20,000) / 20,000 x 100 = -10 per cent
Cost of sales rose 30 per cent (27,000 / 90,000), faster than sales
model.answer: Sales rose 20 per cent but operating profit fell 10 per cent because costs rose faster than revenue.

teach.heading: Using it to decide
bullets: Compare with earlier years to spot trends
Compare gross and operating profit to find where costs rise
Set prices and cost-saving targets
Support a bank loan or investor request
teach.note: Decision-making: a business uses the statement to see where problems are. If gross profit is weak, look at supplier prices, prices charged and waste. If gross profit is fine but operating profit is weak, expenses are the problem. A bank will look at profit to judge whether a loan can be repaid. Ask pupils what Rayyan should look into first and why. Remind them that one year's figures need to be compared with other years or other businesses.

teach.heading: Check: profit calculation
teach.note: Answer C. Gross profit = 80,000 - 50,000 = 30,000; operating profit = 30,000 - 22,000 = 8,000. A is gross profit; B subtracts expenses from revenue skipping cost of sales wrongly; D adds. Show on the board.

check.q: Revenue is 80,000 pounds, cost of sales 50,000 pounds and expenses 22,000 pounds. What is operating profit?
check.why: Gross profit is 80,000 - 50,000 = 30,000. Operating profit = 30,000 - 22,000 = 8,000. 30,000 is only the gross profit.

teach.heading: The nature and importance of profit
bullets: Profit is what is left after costs are paid
It rewards the owners for risk and effort
It can be reinvested to grow the business
It attracts investors and helps secure loans
teach.note: Define profit as revenue minus total costs. Importance: survival (continual losses cannot be sustained), reward for owners, retained profit for growth, confidence for lenders and investors, and funds for pay and community activity. Profit is not the only aim: some businesses are social enterprises. Islamic ethos: trade and earning a fair profit are permitted and praised as ethical enterprise when done honestly; profit must come from lawful, fair dealing, with honest weights and descriptions. Present as general principle only and avoid detailed rulings or quotations unless verified by a scholar.

teach.heading: Misconception: profit is not cash
teach.note: Reinforce the difference. Profit comes from the income statement; cash is the money actually in the bank. Revenue can be recorded when a sale is made but cash may arrive later. A profitable business can still run out of cash if customers pay late or large payments fall due. Link to the cash flow lesson and the liquidity lesson next.

misconception.wrong: If the income statement shows a profit, the business must have plenty of cash.
misconception.right: Profit and cash are different. A business can be profitable but short of cash if customers pay late or it has bought a lot of stock.

teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Madinah Mini Market. Ask: if a supplier asks to be paid tomorrow and the business has stock but little cash, what can it do? Liquidity is about the short term: can it pay wages, suppliers and bills as they fall due? Link to the unit on cash flow. A business can be profitable but illiquid. teach.heading: Two liquidity ratios
teach.note: In the exam the formulae are supplied, but pupils must use them correctly, so practise. Current assets: inventory, receivables (customers who owe money) and cash. Current liabilities: payables (money owed to suppliers), overdraft and other debts due within a year. The acid test removes inventory because it is the slowest to turn into cash. Typical guidance: a current ratio around 1.5 to 2 is often seen as comfortable and an acid test of about 1 or above is safer, but these depend on the type of business, so avoid presenting them as laws.

teach.note: Model carefully. Ask pupils to say it in a sentence. For a supermarket-style business, stock turns quickly so a low acid test may be less worrying; this is a good evaluation point.

teach.heading: Check: acid test
teach.note: Answer A. (50,000 - 20,000) / 15,000 = 2.0. B forgets to subtract inventory (that is the current ratio 3.33). C divides the wrong way round. D subtracts liabilities. Insist on writing the formula first.

check.q: A shop has current assets of 50,000 pounds including inventory of 20,000 pounds, and current liabilities of 15,000 pounds. What is the acid test ratio?
check.why: Acid test = (50,000 - 20,000) / 15,000 = 2.0. 3.3 is the current ratio because inventory has not been removed.

teach.heading: Why liquidity matters, and improving it
bullets: Poor liquidity can mean unpaid wages and suppliers
Suppliers may stop supplying; the business may fail
Too much liquidity means idle cash that could be used
Improve: chase receivables, cut stock, negotiate longer credit, arrange an overdraft
teach.note: Discuss both extremes. Too low: risk of insolvency, even when profitable. Too high: cash or stock sitting unused could be reinvested. Ways to improve: speed up payment by customers, reduce excess inventory, negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers (watch the relationship), arrange a short-term loan or overdraft (has a cost), sell an unused asset. Ask which is best for the mini market and why. Comparing liquidity with earlier years and other businesses is covered in the accounts-analysis lesson.

lessons.bigQuestion: Paper 2 uses a large or multinational business. What changes in your answers compared with Paper 1?
objectives: To understand how to apply knowledge to a large-business case under timed conditions and act on feedback
successCriteria: All: complete a 20-mark Paper 2 style question
Most: improve one answer after feedback
Some: write a 12-mark evaluation with a justified judgement
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty in exams and in self-assessment

keywords.def: define, state, outline, explain, analyse, justify, evaluate: each needs a different kind of answer
a clear decision supported by reasons
a business operating in more than one country

hook.text: Paper 2 uses a large or multinational business. What changes in your answers compared with Paper 1?
hook.a: Scale: economies of scale, structure, exchange rates and global factors become more relevant.

starter.q: Strong pound: a UK exporter's US prices ...

starter.a: choose an option and show why it is better
options: choose an option and show why it is better

teach.heading: Today's case: GreenGrain plc
bullets: A fictional global cereal maker
Factories in three countries
Data on exchange rates, costs and staff
teach.note: On the pupil PDF; mark scheme in the plan.

teach.heading: Feedback from Paper 1 practice
bullets: Strength: calculations with working
Target: use the case in 6-mark answers
Target: finish 12-mark answers with a judgement
teach.note: Adapt to the class's actual scripts.

teach.heading: A strong 12-mark judgement
bullets: Answer the question directly
Say which factor matters most and why
'It depends on ...' with a reason from the case

misconception.wrong: Ending with 'there are advantages and disadvantages'
misconception.right: Make a clear decision and say what it depends on

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: Which is the best 12-mark conclusion?
options: GreenGrain should build in Poland because lower wages outweigh transport costs, as long as the zloty stays stable
check.why: A clear decision, a reason and a condition from the case.

practice.q: Model: 'GreenGrain imports $2.4m of oats. The rate moves from £1 = $1.20 to £1 = $1.50. Calculate the change in cost in pounds. (3)'
A stronger pound helps a UK firm that ...

independent.q: Timed (pupil PDF): complete the GreenGrain 20-mark question; then improve one Paper 1 answer using your feedback in the portal box.
independent.a: Marked against the answer key in the plan; improved answer shows the target met.
independent.model: The teacher shows one improved Paper 1 answer: adding case data to a 6-mark analyse.

independent.q: Extend: write your three revision targets for Spring 2.
independent.a: Three specific targets.

independent.q: Stretch: write a second 12-mark judgement with a different 'it depends on'.
independent.a: An alternative supported judgement.

exit.q: Paper 2 is set in ...
exit.a: a large business

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Paper 2 uses a large or multinational business. What changes in your answers compared with Paper 1?
exit.a: Scale: economies of scale, structure, exchange rates and global factors become more relevant.

lessons.homework: Revise your three targets during the Ramadan break using the pupil PDF revision timetable (20 minutes, three times a week).
lessons.send: SEND: extra time as agreed; reader if on the SEND register. EAL: command-word card. Stretch: top-level 12-mark answer.
